title: Rebalancing and request routing
goal: By the end, you can count how much data each way of moving shards copies when a machine joins, explain how moving shards automatically can turn one overloaded machine into an outage, and follow a request to its shard through any node, a router, or a client that keeps its own map.
opening:
The payments company keeps its payments on ten machines, each payment on machine number `hash mod 10`. The busiest shopping day of the year is a week away, and an eleventh machine has just arrived. The plan fits on one line: switch to `hash mod 11`, and copy every payment whose answer changed to its new machine.

It's easy to think one new machine disturbs one machine's worth of payments, since that's all it needs. The formula doesn't know what the new machine needs. Change 10 to 11, and the answer changes for whichever payments the arithmetic picks. And once payments move, every program that sends a request has to find them again.

Partitioning: consistent hashing and hot keys counted the keys that move when a node joins a ring, and left the copying for later. In this lesson, we'll count what moves under four designs, move whole partitions, and watch an automatic mover take a cluster down. Then we'll follow a request to a payment that moved a minute ago. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: Ten machines hold 100,000 payments, each on machine number `hash mod 10`, the remainder when the payment's hash is divided by 10. You add an eleventh machine and switch to `hash mod 11`. About how many payments now belong on a different machine?
options: About 9,100: the new machine's fair share
About 50,000: half of them
About 91,000: almost all of them
None, until a job runs to move them
warmup.why: A payment stays put only if its hash leaves the same remainder for 10 and for 11. The two remainders repeat every 110 numbers and agree only for 0 to 9, so 10 payments in 110 stay and about 91% move. The demo in the first section counts 91,032. About 9,100 is the tempting answer, because it's the least that has to move, and it's what every other design in this lesson moves. `hash mod N` isn't one of them.

sections.h: Adding one machine to hash mod N moves almost every payment
sections.body:
Splitting data: key ranges, hashes and tenants placed payments with `hash mod N`. Hash the payment's key into a big random-looking number, divide by N, the number of machines, and keep the remainder. But N doesn't stay put. You add machines before a busy season, replace one whose disk failed, and retire old ones. Each change of N changes the answer for most keys.

Work it out for 10 machines going to 11. Call a key's hash h. The key stays where it is only if `h mod 10` equals `h mod 11`. Both remainders repeat every 110 numbers, and they agree only for the first 10 numbers of each run of 110, 0 to 9. So 10 keys in 110 stay put, and the other 100 in 110, about 91%, move. The demo below counts 91,032 of 100,000.

Moving a key isn't free. Its bytes cross the network from the old machine to the new one, while both keep answering card payments. Say the cluster, the group of machines working as one store, holds 3 TB. Then 91% is 2.7 TB of copying to add one machine. The new machine only needs its fair share, 1/11 of the data, about 270 GB. That's the least any design can move, and everything above it is waste: payments going from machine 3 to machine 7 when neither of them is new.

That sets the target for this lesson. Moving data between machines so that each holds a fair share is called **rebalancing**, and a good design rebalances like this when a machine joins:

- it moves about 1/(N+1) of the data, the new machine's fair share;
- everything that moves goes to the new machine;
- many old machines share the sending, so no single disk or network link does all of it.

The ring from the last lesson gets close. A node is one machine in the group, and a token is one of its places on the ring. With 16 tokens per node, the demo moves 10.2% of the keys, all to the new node, from 9 senders. With one token per node, it moves 9.2%, all from a single sender. A partition is another word for a shard. The next two sections cover the designs real stores use: a fixed number of partitions, partitions that split as they grow, and partition counts that grow with the nodes. The last section asks the question that moving raises: once a payment has moved, how does a request find it?

try.title: Count what moves when an eleventh node joins
steps: Read `RebalanceDemo.kt`. It places 100,000 payment keys on 10 nodes four ways: `hash mod N`, 1,000 fixed partitions (the next section), a ring with 1 token per node and a ring with 16. Then it adds `node-11` and counts the keys whose owner changed, how many of them went to the new node, and how many old nodes sent them.
Predict the percentage for `hash mod N`, and which design has a single sender.
Run it from the `labs` folder. No Docker needed.

code.title: RebalanceDemo.kt

try.expect:
```text
hash mod N                 91,032 keys move (91.0%),  9,150 of them to node-11, sent by 10 nodes
1,000 fixed partitions      8,955 keys move ( 9.0%),  8,955 of them to node-11, sent by 10 nodes
ring, 1 token(s) per node   9,212 keys move ( 9.2%),  9,212 of them to node-11, sent by  1 node
ring, 16 token(s) per node 10,230 keys move (10.2%), 10,230 of them to node-11, sent by  9 nodes
```

`hash mod N` moves 91% of the keys, and only 9,150 of those 91,032 go to the new node: the rest trade places between old nodes. The other three move close to the ideal 9.1%, all of it to `node-11`. One token per node puts all the sending on one neighbour. Fixed partitions spread it over all ten old nodes, and the 16-token ring over nine.

sections.h: Fixed partitions: far more partitions than machines, moved whole
sections.body:
Picture the left-luggage office at a big station, with 1,000 numbered lockers and ten attendants, each looking after 100 lockers. A traveller's locker number is stamped on their key and never changes. When an eleventh attendant starts, the manager hands her the keys to 90 lockers, about nine from each of the others. No locker moves, and no traveller gets a new number.

Let's build that. Splitting data had a first map, from a key to its shard. Split it into two steps. First, hash each key to one of P partitions with `hash mod P`. P is chosen once, when the system is created, and it's much bigger than the number of nodes: say 1,000 partitions for 10 nodes. Second, keep a table from partition to node, 100 partitions each. A key's partition never changes, because P never changes. When an eleventh node joins, it takes whole partitions from the others until it holds its share, 90 of them, about nine from each old node. Only the keys in those 90 partitions move: 8,955 of 100,000 in the demo, the minimum, sent by all ten old nodes.

A partition is a natural unit to move. It's a set of files, or a log, that the old node can copy across while it keeps serving. Then the table changes the partition's owner to the new node. The stepper walks through one join. Here the lockers picture breaks: handing over a key takes a second, while moving a partition copies gigabytes between machines that are busy serving, and the copying itself loads the nodes it's meant to relieve.

This is the most common design. Kafka, a program that keeps logs of messages, splits each topic, a named log, into a fixed number of partitions. A producer, the program that writes messages, picks a key's partition by hashing the key mod that number, and Kafka moves whole partitions between its servers. Elasticsearch and OpenSearch, two search engines, keep documents in indexes, and fix an index's number of primary shards (the main copy of each shard) when you create it. They send each document to `hash(_routing) % number_of_primary_shards`, where `_routing` is the document's id unless you set it. Redis, a fast store that keeps its data in memory, spreads keys over a cluster in 16,384 hash slots. Those are fixed partitions too (Redis Cluster and production operations, in the Caching track). And Notion, the notes app from Splitting data, runs 480 logical shards: fixed partitions over PostgreSQL, a free database program. Going from 32 machines to 96 moved whole shards between machines, and no workspace changed shard.

Notion chose 480 because it divides evenly by many numbers, for the same reason an hour has 60 minutes. With P partitions on N nodes, the busiest node holds P/N, rounded up. 480 spreads perfectly over 32, 40, 48 or 96 machines. 512 spreads perfectly only over powers of two (2, 4, 8 and so on). On 96 machines, some hold 6 and some hold 5, and the busiest carries 13% more than the average.

The price is that P is chosen once. Too few, and you hit a wall: with 12 partitions, a 13th node has nothing to hold, and more nodes stop helping. Too many, and every partition's fixed cost adds up, as the box below explains. And changing P later means rehashing keys. In Kafka, adding partitions changes `hash mod P` for most keys. A key's new messages then go to a different partition from its old ones, and the order of one key's messages breaks. Elasticsearch makes you split, shrink or reindex, which means copying every document into a new index. **Pick P once, for the size you expect years from now, with plenty of divisors.** Next, we'll meet stores that can't fix P at all.

aside.title: Why not pick a huge number, like a million partitions?
aside.body: Every partition costs something even when it's nearly empty: its own files, a line in every copy of the map, and often its own leader to keep alive. Elastic's sizing guidance aims for shards of 10 to 50 GB, because each shard runs its part of a search on one thread, one path of work, so thousands of tiny shards use up the threads that all searches share. A million partitions also make a map that every router has to hold and keep up to date. So stores pick a number that is large but not huge. Redis Cluster's 16,384 slots are one example, and they also cap a Redis Cluster at 16,384 primaries.

sections.h: Partitions that split as they grow, and the danger of moving them automatically
sections.body:
Stores that keep keys in sorted ranges, like the key-range shards of Splitting data, can't fix their partition count in advance. A range holds whatever keys fall into it, and nobody knows that ahead of time. So these stores split. A range that grows past a size limit is cut in two at its middle key. HBase, a database that keeps rows in sorted ranges, splits at 10 GiB. CockroachDB, a database that spreads its tables over many machines, splits at 512 MiB. It also merges neighbours that shrink below 128 MiB, and splits a range that gets too busy, so two nodes can share a busy range. MongoDB, a popular database that stores records as documents, works in ranges of about 128 MB, which its balancer, the part that evens out data between shards, splits and moves.

The number of partitions now follows the data: a small table has a few, and a big one has thousands. A split moves nothing between machines by itself. It makes a new unit that can move, and a new node takes whole ranges, just as with fixed partitions.

Cassandra, the ring-based database from the last lesson, takes a third path: the number of partitions grows with the nodes. Each node owns 16 token ranges, so 10 nodes make 160 ranges, and an 11th node adds 16 more by splitting existing ones (Partitioning: consistent hashing and hot keys). A partition's size grows with the data per node, not with the data in total.

Who decides when to move a partition? The store can do it on its own, or it can propose a plan for a person to approve. Moving on its own is convenient, and it fails in one particular way. Every node sends a short "I'm alive" message, a heartbeat, every second or so. A failure detector declares a node dead when its heartbeats stop arriving in time.

Now suppose a node is overloaded, by a hot partition, say. Its replies slow down, its heartbeats arrive late, and the failure detector decides it's dead. The rebalancer moves its partitions to the others, which were already busy. Now they're overloaded, their heartbeats slip, and they're declared dead too. That's a **cascading failure**: the fix spreads the overload. The Try it runs it on five nodes, each at 88% of what it can handle. One partition triples. Two seconds later the automatic cluster serves nothing, while the cluster that only alerted a person still serves 4,520 of 4,840 requests a second.

So many systems keep a person in the loop when nodes join or leave. Dynamo, Amazon's 2007 design that Cassandra copied, made adding or removing a node an explicit command from an operator, the person running the system. Then a node that drops out for a few minutes doesn't start a flood of copying. Couchbase and Riak, two other databases, propose a new plan and wait for an administrator to approve it. MongoDB's balancer moves on its own, but carefully: a shard takes part in only one move at a time, and you can limit balancing to a window of quiet hours. For a peak you can see coming, the busiest shopping day or a big ticket sale, rebalance by hand beforehand, while the cluster is quiet.

Moving is only half the job. Next, every request has to find the partition's new home.

try.title: Watch automatic rebalancing take a cluster down
steps: Read `CascadeDemo.kt`. Five nodes hold 20 partitions of 220 requests a second each: 880 per node, against a limit of 1,000. At second 1, partition 7 on node-3 jumps to 660. A node over its limit misses its health checks and is called dead. One policy moves a dead node's partitions to the least busy survivors; the other only alerts a person.
Predict how many seconds the automatic cluster lasts.

code.title: CascadeDemo.kt

try.expect:
```text
automatic: move a dead node's partitions to the others
  second 0: node-1=880 node-2=880 node-3=880 node-4=880 node-5=880  served 4,400 of 4,400 a second
  second 1: node-1=880 node-2=880 node-3=1320 node-4=880 node-5=880  served 4,520 of 4,840 a second
  second 2: node-1=1100 node-2=1540 node-4=1100 node-5=1100  served 4,000 of 4,840 a second
  second 3: no nodes left  served 0 of 4,840 a second
manual: alert a person, move nothing
  second 0: node-1=880 node-2=880 node-3=880 node-4=880 node-5=880  served 4,400 of 4,400 a second
  second 1: node-1=880 node-2=880 node-3=1320 node-4=880 node-5=880  served 4,520 of 4,840 a second
  second 2: node-1=880 node-2=880 node-3=1320 node-4=880 node-5=880  served 4,520 of 4,840 a second
  second 3: node-1=880 node-2=880 node-3=1320 node-4=880 node-5=880  served 4,520 of 4,840 a second
```

At second 1, node-3 is over its limit and drops 320 requests a second. The automatic policy calls it dead and hands its four partitions (1,320 a second) to the other four nodes. Each was at 880, so every one of them goes over 1,000, and at second 3 the whole cluster is "dead". The manual policy keeps losing 320 a second on one node, 7% of traffic, until a person moves or splits partition 7. The model is crude: real failure detectors wait several seconds, and real moves take minutes of copying, which adds load. But real cascades have the same shape.

sections.h: Finding the shard: ask any node, ask a router, or keep the map yourself
sections.body:
Partitions move, so a program can't hard-code where a key lives. Something has to hold the second map, from partition to node, and every request has to use it. At the left-luggage office, a traveller can ask any attendant, who walks them to the right one. They can ask at a front desk that knows every locker. Or they can carry a map of their own. Stores use all three, as the figure shows.

Ask any node. The client, the program sending the request, sends it to any node, and that node forwards it to the right one. Cassandra works this way. Whichever node receives a request becomes its coordinator, and every node keeps the whole token map. The nodes spread changes to that map by gossip, passing news to a few others each second until everyone knows; lesson 5 of this track covers it.

Ask a router. The client talks to a routing tier, a router that knows the map and stores no data. MongoDB's router, `mongos`, keeps a copy of the map of ranges from the config servers, a small group of machines that stores the cluster's own information. It sends each query to the shards that hold its ranges, and a query without the shard key goes to all of them. Figma, the design-tool company from Splitting data, built DBProxy. It reads each SQL query, a request in the language most databases speak, and sends it on by its shard key. Vitess does the same for MySQL, another popular free database.

Keep the map yourself. A partition-aware client's library keeps its own copy of the map and goes straight to the owner, which saves a hop. Cassandra's drivers, the libraries programs use to talk to it, can work out a key's token and pick a node that holds it. A Kafka producer fetches the cluster's metadata, its information about itself, which names the leader of each partition, the server that takes its writes. It fetches it again when a server answers that it's no longer the leader. A Redis Cluster client keeps the slot map, the table of which server owns each slot.

Wherever the lookups happen, the true map has to live somewhere everyone agrees on, or two routers can each believe a different node owns a partition. Many systems keep it in a consensus store, a small group of machines that changes its data only when most of them agree. ZooKeeper and etcd are two well-known ones, and Kafka and several newer databases build one in. The Consistency and consensus track builds these.

Every copy of the map goes stale the moment a partition moves. So the real design question is what a node does with a request for a key it no longer owns. Redis Cluster's answer, from the Caching track, is the cleanest to study. A node that doesn't own the key's slot answers `MOVED <slot> <node>`: the slot lives there now, so update your map and try there. While a slot is being moved, its old owner still answers for the keys it has. For keys already copied, it answers `ASK <slot> <node>`. The client sends that one request to the new node, after the command `ASKING`, and leaves its map alone, because most of the slot is still on the old owner. When the move ends, the old owner answers `MOVED`, once per client, and the maps catch up. **No request fails during a move: each one costs at most one extra hop.** The lab builds that client.

Every request in this lesson carried its key, so the map could send it to one shard. Not every question names the key the data was split by.

try.title: Trace three reads through a slot migration
steps: Read `RedirectDemo.kt`. Three nodes share 16 slots; slot 0 starts on A and holds three keys. The client reads all three before the move, after one key has been copied to C, and after the move ends. Each line prints every hop and the client's map entry for slot 0.
Predict which reads get `ASK`, which get `MOVED`, and when the client's map changes.

code.title: RedirectDemo.kt

try.expect:
```text
before the migration
  GET pay-103 -> A: "value of pay-103"   (client map: slot 0 on A)
  GET pay-117 -> A: "value of pay-117"   (client map: slot 0 on A)
  GET pay-159 -> A: "value of pay-159"   (client map: slot 0 on A)
slot 0 starts moving to C; pay-103 has been copied
  GET pay-103 -> A: ASK 0 C -> ASKING, C: "value of pay-103"   (client map: slot 0 on A)
  GET pay-117 -> A: "value of pay-117"   (client map: slot 0 on A)
  GET pay-159 -> A: "value of pay-159"   (client map: slot 0 on A)
the rest are copied, and C owns slot 0
  GET pay-103 -> A: MOVED 0 C -> C: "value of pay-103"   (client map: slot 0 on C)
  GET pay-117 -> C: "value of pay-117"   (client map: slot 0 on C)
  GET pay-159 -> C: "value of pay-159"   (client map: slot 0 on C)
```

During the move, only the copied key costs a hop, and the client's map still says A, which is right for the two keys A still holds. After the move, the first read gets `MOVED`, the map flips to C, and the next two reads go straight there. Every read returned its value. The model uses 16 slots and MD5; Redis uses 16,384 slots and a checksum called CRC16, with the same replies.

worked.title: Choose the number of logical shards for a sharded payments table

steps.say: Start from the growth, not from today's machines. The payments table holds 3 TB, grows by 40 GB a day, and each PostgreSQL machine should hold at most 500 GB.
steps.code:
today        3 TB                       -> 6 machines at 500 GB
in 3 years   3 TB + 40 GB x 1,095 days  = about 46.8 TB
             46.8 TB / 500 GB          -> about 94 machines

steps.say: So the count has to spread evenly over anything from 6 to about 100 machines, with a few shards per machine even at the top. Then one busy machine can be relieved by moving one or two shards. Compare the candidates by how much more the busiest machine holds than the average.

Read the result. 480 is perfectly even at every count from 6 to 96 machines. 720 is uneven at 32 and 96 (720 / 96 = 7.5, so some machines hold 8 and some 7). 256 and 512 are even only at powers of two, and at 96 machines the busiest carries 13% more than the average. Pick 480.

Keep the routing table small and in one place. Each logical shard is a schema, a named group of tables, and the table maps each shard number to a database machine. Moving a shard goes like this: copy the schema to the new machine, catch up on the changes made since then from the old machine's stream of changes, pause writes to that one shard for a moment, flip the table entry, and carry on. Every other shard keeps working.

lab.title: Rebalance two ways, then follow MOVED and ASK
steps: Run the tests from the `labs` folder. No Docker needed. 13 of 15 fail with `NotImplementedError`, Kotlin's error for code that isn't written yet. Two pass already: the `hash mod N` count, which uses the given `ModN`, and the new owner's reply to a request without `ASKING`, which tests the given `Cluster`.

In `Placement.kt`, write `FixedPartitions.addNode`: move one partition at a time from the busiest node to the new one, until the new one holds its fair share. Watch the property test, which tries many node and partition counts: every node must end with the fair share, rounded down or up.

In `DynamicRanges.kt`, write `insert`: add the key to its range, and split a range that passes `maxKeys` at its median key, the middle one. The test with time-ordered keys checks that every insert lands in the last range, however often it splits.
In `Redirects.kt`, write `RoutingClient.get`: follow `MOVED` (update the map) and `ASK` (one request with `asking = true`, map unchanged). All 15 pass.

Experiment: change your `Ask` branch so it also writes the new node into `slotMap`. Run the tests and read which one fails, and why. The client now sends the keys still on A to C, which bounces them back with `MOVED`. Put it back.
hints: `addNode`: count the partitions per node first (`owner.forEach { counts.merge(it, 1, Int::plus) }`), then loop while the new node holds fewer than `partitionCount / nodes.size`. The giver is the node with the most, and on a tie the one whose name sorts first: `compareBy<Map.Entry<String, Int>> { it.value }.thenByDescending { it.key }`.
The giver's highest partition is `owner.indices.last { owner[it] == donor }`.

`insert`: `range.keys.elementAt(range.keys.size / 2)` is the median. `range.keys.tailSet(median, true)` is a live view of the upper half: copy it into the new range's keys, then `clear()` the view to remove those keys from the old range. Put the new range in `byStart` under the median.

`get`: loop at most six times. Keep `node` and `asking` in local variables. On `Moved`, set `slotMap[reply.slot] = reply.node` and `asking = false`; on `Ask`, set `asking = true` and touch nothing else.

drill.title: The redirect loop from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write `get(key)` for a client that has a `slotMap: Array<String>` and a `send(node, key, asking): Reply`, where `Reply` is `Value(v)`, `Moved(slot, node)` or `Ask(slot, node)`. Then say in one sentence why `Ask` must not update the map.

recap: `hash mod N` moves about N/(N+1) of the keys when a machine joins: 91% going from 10 to 11. A good design moves about 1/(N+1), all of it to the new machine, from many senders.

Fixed partitions (Kafka, Elasticsearch and OpenSearch, Redis Cluster's 16,384 slots, Notion's 480) hash keys to P partitions once and move whole partitions. Choose P large and with many divisors, because it's hard to change later.

Stores with sorted ranges split them as they grow (HBase at 10 GiB, CockroachDB at 512 MiB and when a range gets too busy, MongoDB's 128 MB ranges). Cassandra's partition count grows with the nodes, 16 ranges each.

Moving partitions automatically can cascade: an overloaded node is called dead, its load lands on the others, and they fail in turn. Keep a person in the loop for joins and leaves, and rebalance before a peak you can see coming.

Requests find shards through any node (Cassandra), a router (mongos, Figma's DBProxy, Vitess) or a client that keeps the map (Cassandra drivers, Kafka, Redis Cluster). Redis Cluster's MOVED fixes a stale map; ASK sends one request to the new owner during a move and leaves the map alone.
The limit: every map here routes by the partition key. A question that names something else, such as a card instead of a payment, has to ask every shard.
closing:
We started with an eleventh machine and a plan that would have moved nine payments in ten. Fixed partitions move only the new machine's share, in whole pieces, and MOVED and ASK keep every request finding its payment while the pieces travel.

If you have the three-node Redis Cluster from Redis Cluster and production operations running, run `redis-cli -p 7001 GET payment:42`. If that key's slot lives on another node, you'll get a MOVED error naming it (if not, try a few other keys). Then add `-c`, which makes redis-cli follow redirects, and watch it hop.

Next, we'll look payments up by card instead of by payment number, and find out how many shards one question has to ask when it doesn't carry the key.

quiz.q: A store has 64 fixed partitions and grows from 32 machines to 80. What happens?
options: 16 of the new machines hold no partition, so they add nothing for this data
The partitions split by themselves into 80
Every key is rehashed into 80 partitions
Each machine ends up with 0.8 of a partition
quiz.why: A partition is the smallest unit that moves, and 64 partitions can fill at most 64 machines. Stores with fixed partitions don't split partitions or rehash keys by themselves; raising P means a split or a reindex. This is the wall you hit when P is chosen too small.

quiz.q: One partition on node-3 gets busy, and node-3's replies slow down past the failure detector's timeout. The store moves partitions automatically when it decides a node has failed. What is the risk?
options: None: moving node-3's partitions away is the right fix
node-3 loses its data, because it was declared dead
The busy partition splits by itself and the load disappears
node-3's load, busy partition included, lands on nodes that were already busy, which overload and get declared dead in turn
quiz.why: The node isn't dead, it's slow. Moving its partitions adds its whole load, plus the work of copying, to the survivors. If they were near their limit, they slow down too, and the rebalancer repeats the mistake. That's why Dynamo made joining and leaving an explicit command from an operator.

quiz.q: During a slot move, a Redis Cluster client gets `ASK 0 C` for a key. What should it do?
options: Update its map to say slot 0 is on C, then try again there
Send `ASKING`, then the command, to C, and keep its map saying slot 0 is on the old owner
Keep asking the old owner until the key comes back
Fetch the whole slot map again from every node
quiz.why: ASK means this one key has already been copied, while most of the slot is still on the old owner. Updating the map would send every other key of slot 0 to C, which would bounce them back with MOVED. Only MOVED, which means the slot has moved for good, updates the map.

quiz.q: A MongoDB collection (MongoDB's word for a table) is sharded on `{ merchantId: 1 }`, the shop's id. A query asks only for `cardFingerprint`, a value that identifies a card without its number, and that field has an index. What does `mongos`, MongoDB's router, do?
options: Sends it to the one shard whose range contains the fingerprint
Asks the config servers to run it
Sends it to every shard of the collection; each uses its own index, and mongos merges the results
Rejects it, because mongos only routes by shard key
quiz.why: The ranges are ranges of the shard key, so a fingerprint says nothing about which shard holds the rows. mongos sends the query to every shard, each shard uses its best local index, and mongos merges the answers. Secondary indexes across shards, the next lesson, is about exactly this cost.

quiz.q: From Partitioning: consistent hashing and hot keys. A Cassandra cluster with 16 tokens per node gets an eleventh node. Which is true?
options: It takes about 1/11 of the data, in small slices from several existing nodes
It takes half of one neighbour's data
Every key is rehashed, as with `hash mod N`
It takes nothing until a repair runs
quiz.why: Each of the new node's 16 tokens takes the slice just before it from whichever node owned it, so the new node gets about its fair share, from several senders. Half of one neighbour is the one-token case at its worst, and rehashing everything is `hash mod N`.

flashcards.front: How many keys move when `hash mod N` goes from 10 to 11 machines?
flashcards.back: About 10 in 11 (91%): a key stays only if its hash leaves the same remainder for 10 and for 11.

flashcards.front: What's the least data a new machine can make move?
flashcards.back: Its fair share, 1/(N+1) of the data, all of it to the new machine.

flashcards.front: Fixed partitions: what changes when a node joins?
flashcards.back: Only the table from partition to node. Whole partitions move; a key's partition never changes.

flashcards.front: Why did Notion pick 480 logical shards?
flashcards.back: 480 divides evenly by many machine counts (32, 40, 48, 96 and more), so every machine holds the same number of shards. 512 is even only at powers of two.

flashcards.front: How can automatic rebalancing cause an outage?
flashcards.back: An overloaded node is declared dead; its load moves onto others, which overload and are declared dead in turn: a cascading failure.

flashcards.front: MOVED or ASK: which one updates the client's slot map?
flashcards.back: MOVED: the slot has moved for good. ASK is for one key during a move: send `ASKING` plus the command to the new owner, and keep the map.

flashcards.front: Three places to send a request to its shard?
flashcards.back: Any node, which forwards it (Cassandra); a router (mongos, Vitess, Figma's DBProxy); a client that keeps the map (Cassandra drivers, Kafka clients, Redis Cluster clients).

terms.plain: Moving data between nodes so that each holds a fair share, for example when a node joins or leaves.
A partition count chosen once and much larger than the node count. Keys never change partition, and whole partitions move between nodes.
Cutting a range in two when it grows past a size limit (or gets too busy), so the number of partitions follows the data.
A failure that spreads because the reaction to it, such as moving load onto other nodes, overloads them too.
A layer of routers that knows which node holds each partition and forwards requests, holding no data itself, like MongoDB's mongos.
A client library that keeps its own copy of the partition map and sends each request straight to the owner.
Redis Cluster's reply meaning the key's slot lives on another node now: update your map and try there.
Redis Cluster's reply during a slot move, meaning this key has already moved: send ASKING and this one request to the new node, and keep your map.

explain_back.prompt: Your team splits the payments table over 8 PostgreSQL machines with `hash(merchant_id) mod 8`, and now needs 4 more machines. Explain why that's painful, and what you'd have done differently.
explain_back.answer: With `hash mod 8`, going to 12 machines changes the remainder for most shops. A shop stays only if its hash leaves the same remainder for 8 and for 12, which happens for 8 out of every 24 hash values, a third. So about two thirds of the data has to be copied, much of it between old machines that gain nothing, all while payments keep arriving. And during the move, every router has to know which shops have moved, shop by shop. If we'd started with fixed logical shards, say 480 schemas with 60 on each of the 8 machines, a shop's logical shard would never change. Adding 4 machines would move 160 whole schemas, 40 to each new machine. That's a third of the data, all of it to new machines, and the routing table would change one schema at a time. 480 also spreads evenly over 8, 12, 16 or 24 machines. We'd keep that table in one place that every router reads, and move shards one at a time by hand, outside the busy season.

deeper.body:
The stores in this lesson have made moving data a first-class operation, something you ask for with one command.

MongoDB 8.0 added `moveCollection` (move an unsharded collection to another shard), `unshardCollection`, and resharding to the same shard key as a way to spread data out again. Resharding writes to all shards at the same time, while the balancer's moves are limited to one per shard at a time. Percona, a company that supports MongoDB, measured a reshard of a few gigabytes at about 3 minutes on MongoDB 7.0 and under 1 minute on 8.0, on an idle cluster.

Redis 8.4 and Valkey 9.0 (a free fork of Redis, a copy that's developed separately) added atomic slot migration, which moves a whole slot as one operation instead of key by key. Clients still have to understand MOVED, but the window in which ASK appears shrinks.

Elasticsearch and OpenSearch can split an index into a multiple of its primary shard count, or shrink it to a factor of it, without rewriting every document. Any other change of the shard count is a reindex.

Cassandra 6.0, still at an early test stage (alpha), moves the token map out of gossip and into a metadata service run by consensus, so that every node agrees on it.

Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 7 has a good section on the open problems of request routing. Who decides the assignment without split brain, two parts of the cluster each believing it's in charge? How do routers learn about changes? And what happens to requests that are in flight at the switch? The Consistency and consensus track answers the first question, and this lesson's MOVED and ASK are one answer to the third.
